claim: The transition from prokaryotic to eukaryotic evolution is poorly understood due to a lack of reliable intermediate forms.
source: The transition from pro- to eukaryote evolution is poorly understood due to a lack of reliable intermediate forms and definitions regarding the nature of the first host that could no longer be considered a prokaryote, the first eukaryotic common ancestor, FECA.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific understanding in the field.

claim: LECA was a complex cell that united all traits characterising eukaryotic biology including a mitochondrion.
source: The last eukaryotic common ancestor, LECA, was a complex cell that united all traits characterising eukaryotic biology including a mitochondrion.
evidence: This represents the current scientific consensus about LECA based on phylogenomic and cell biological studies.

claim: The discovery of the asgard archaea has stimulated discussions regarding the pre-endosymbiotic complexity of FECA.
source: In particular the discovery of the asgard archaea has stimulated discussions regarding the pre-endosymbiotic complexity of FECA.
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of asgard archaea discovery on the field.

claim: Eukaryotic cell biology evolved as a solution to housing a semi-autonomous organelle.
source: Inspecting eukaryotic traits from the perspective of the endosymbiont uncovers that eukaryotic cell biology can be explained as having evolved as a solution to housing a semi-autonomous organelle and why the addition of another endosymbiont, the plastid, added no extra compartments.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the manuscript, supported by inference from multiple lines of evidence discussed throughout.

claim: The addition of the plastid endosymbiont added no extra compartments to eukaryotic cells.
source: Inspecting eukaryotic traits from the perspective of the endosymbiont uncovers that eukaryotic cell biology can be explained as having evolved as a solution to housing a semi-autonomous organelle and why the addition of another endosymbiont, the plastid, added no extra compartments.
evidence: This is supported by observations of plastid acquisition in various lineages.

claim: Mitochondria provided the selective pressures for the origin and continued maintenance of eukaryotic cell complexity.
source: Mitochondria provided the selective pressures for the origin (and continued maintenance) of eukaryotic cell complexity.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the manuscript, supported by inference from multiple observations.

claim: Mitochondria provided the energetic benefit throughout eukaryogenesis for evolving thousands of gene families unique to eukaryotes.
source: Moreover, they also provided the energetic benefit throughout eukaryogenesis for evolving thousands of gene families unique to eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by bioenergetic arguments and observations about eukaryote-specific gene families.

claim: The Golgi apparatus, nucleus, autophagosomes, and meiosis and sex evolved as a response to the selective pressures an endosymbiont imposes.
source: Hence, a synthesis of the current data lets us conclude that traits such as the Golgi apparatus, the nucleus, autophagosomes, and meiosis and sex evolved as a response to the selective pressures an endosymbiont imposes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on synthesis of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea.
source: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea (Fox et al., 1980; Koga et al., 1998; Woese et al., 1990) and document the dichotomy of pro- and eukaryotes, which is further evident in the number of protein families (Rebeaud et al., 2021), average protein length (Brocchieri and Karlin, 2005), cellular and morphological complexity (Stanier et al., 1963), and the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass (Bar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited phylogenetic and biochemical studies.

claim: The prokaryote-eukaryote dichotomy is evident in the number of protein families.
source: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea (Fox et al., 1980; Koga et al., 1998; Woese et al., 1990) and document the dichotomy of pro- and eukaryotes, which is further evident in the number of protein families (Rebeaud et al., 2021), average protein length (Brocchieri and Karlin, 2005), cellular and morphological complexity (Stanier et al., 1963), and the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass (Bar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on protein families.

claim: The prokaryote-eukaryote dichotomy is evident in average protein length.
source: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea (Fox et al., 1980; Koga et al., 1998; Woese et al., 1990) and document the dichotomy of pro- and eukaryotes, which is further evident in the number of protein families (Rebeaud et al., 2021), average protein length (Brocchieri and Karlin, 2005), cellular and morphological complexity (Stanier et al., 1963), and the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass (Bar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on protein length.

claim: The prokaryote-eukaryote dichotomy is evident in cellular and morphological complexity.
source: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea (Fox et al., 1980; Koga et al., 1998; Woese et al., 1990) and document the dichotomy of pro- and eukaryotes, which is further evident in the number of protein families (Rebeaud et al., 2021), average protein length (Brocchieri and Karlin, 2005), cellular and morphological complexity (Stanier et al., 1963), and the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass (Bar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on cellular complexity.

claim: The prokaryote-eukaryote dichotomy is evident in the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass.
source: Phylogeny and biochemistry separate prokaryotes into bacteria and archaea (Fox et al., 1980; Koga et al., 1998; Woese et al., 1990) and document the dichotomy of pro- and eukaryotes, which is further evident in the number of protein families (Rebeaud et al., 2021), average protein length (Brocchieri and Karlin, 2005), cellular and morphological complexity (Stanier et al., 1963), and the overall prevalent contribution to the planet's biomass (Bar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on biomass contribution.

claim: The search for archezoa focused on a eukaryotic phylum lacking a mitochondrion.
source: For curious reasons (see Martin et al., 2017a, for details) this search focused on a eukaryotic phylum lacking a mitochondrion (Cavalier-Smith, 1987; Speijer, 2020), but not necessarily one lacking a nucleus or endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is a historical account supported by citations.

claim: Hydrogenosomes and mitosomes are reduced mitochondria.
source: Through the identification of hydrogenosomes and mitosomes (reduced mitochondria; Tovar et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2002) and modern phylogenomics (Burki et al., 2020), we now understand that the biology of LECA matched that of extant garden variety protists.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies identifying these organelles.

claim: The biology of LECA matched that of extant garden variety protists.
source: Through the identification of hydrogenosomes and mitosomes (reduced mitochondria; Tovar et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2002) and modern phylogenomics (Burki et al., 2020), we now understand that the biology of LECA matched that of extant garden variety protists.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic studies and organelle identification.

claim: LECA evolved from an archaeal host cell and its endosymbiotic alphaproteobacterial partner.
source: LECA evolved from an archaeal host cell and its endosymbiotic alphaproteobacterial partner (Imachi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017) and could have been syncytial and fungus-like, with the first gametes budding off as a selectable unit, in what one could describe to be a flagellated protist (Garg and Martin, 2016; Skejo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on eukaryogenesis.

claim: LECA could have been syncytial and fungus-like, with the first gametes budding off as a selectable unit.
source: LECA evolved from an archaeal host cell and its endosymbiotic alphaproteobacterial partner (Imachi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017) and could have been syncytial and fungus-like, with the first gametes budding off as a selectable unit, in what one could describe to be a flagellated protist (Garg and Martin, 2016; Skejo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited theoretical work.

claim: The transition between prokaryotes and eukaryotes was fluid in nature, with the emergence of new traits occurring in a currently unknown order.
source: The transition between prokaryotes and eukaryotes was fluid in nature, with the emergence of the new traits occurring in a currently unknown order (Gould et al., 2016; López-García and Moreira, 2020; Vosseberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on eukaryogenesis.

claim: Mitochondria-early theories place endosymbiosis closer to or at FECA.
source: Briefly, mitochondria-early theories place endosymbiosis closer to or at FECA (Figure 1), suggesting that the traits that characterize LECA evolved after endosymbiosis from a prokaryotic-like host cell.
evidence: This is a description of a class of theoretical models, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Mitochondria-late scenarios view endosymbiosis and mitochondrial origin as a finishing touch to the LECA.
source: On the contrary, mitochondria-late scenarios view endosymbiosis and mitochondrial origin as a finishing touch to the LECA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of a class of theoretical models, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The notion that eukaryote-like complexity was a prerequisite to phagocytosis for promoting mitochondrial origin remains unsubstantiated.
source: The notion that eukaryote-like complexity was a prerequisite to phagocytosis for promoting mitochondrial origin appears mandatory to some, but the idea remains unsubstantiated (Leão et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2017b; Mills, 2020; Shiratori et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited critical analyses of the phagocytosis-first hypothesis.

claim: Reports of ESCRT-III, ubiquitin modifying system, and eukaryote-like actin in the TACK superphylum triggered thoughts about phagocytosing archaea.
source: Reports of a patchy distribution of homologues of the eukaryotic ESCRT-III, a ubiquitin modifying system, and eukaryote-like actin in the TACK superphylum, triggered thoughts about phagocytosing archaea (Guy and Ettema, 2011; Yutin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a historical account of how certain genomic findings influenced thinking in the field.

claim: The identification of proteins with homology to ESCRT I and II, longin domains, sec23 and sec24 in asgard archaea led to speculations about complex asgard archaea.
source: The identification of proteins with homology to ESCRT I and II, longin domains, sec23 and sec24 (Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017), Rab-like GTPase (Akıl and Robinson, 2018; Klinger et al., 2016; Surkont and Pereira-Leal, 2016), or profilin that can inhibit (in vitro) rabbit actin polymerization (Akıl and Robinson, 2018; Survery et al., 2021) quickly channelled into speculations that asgard archaea might have a dynamic cytoskeleton, intracellular membrane trafficking, and are morphologically complex (Klinger et al., 2016; Neveu et al., 2020; Zachar et al., 2018; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes how genomic findings led to speculative interpretations, supported by citations.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy of Prometheoarchaeon syntrophicum revealed tiny prokaryotes with no intracellular eukaryotic traits living in syntrophy with bacteria.
source: When transmission electron microscopy revealed images of asgard archaea, that of Prometheoarchaeon syntrophicum, they uncovered tiny prokaryotes with no intracellular eukaryotic traits living in syntrophy with bacteria (Imachi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on direct microscopic observation reported in the cited study.

claim: Images of Prometheoarchaeon syntrophicum contradict the narrative of complex asgard archaea.
source: Such images contradict the narrative of complex asgard archaea, but resonate well with early warnings regarding overinterpretations of metagenome data (Dey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing microscopy data with previous speculations.

claim: Among eukaryotic genomes there are more genes of bacterial than of archaeal origin.
source: Among eukaryotic genomes there are more genes of bacterial than of archaeal origin (Alvarez-Ponce et al., 2013; Brueckner and Martin, 2020; Makarova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited phylogenomic studies.

claim: An autogenous origin of cellular complexity on the basis of an archaeal host source alone would predict more archaeal than bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes.
source: Among eukaryotic genomes there are more genes of bacterial than of archaeal origin (Alvarez-Ponce et al., 2013; Brueckner and Martin, 2020; Makarova et al., 2005). An autogenous origin of cellular complexity on the basis of an archaeal (host) source alone would predict the opposite but prokaryotes are characterized by mosaic genomes due to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) whose contribution to cellular complexity prior to endosymbiosis is debated (Martin et al., 2017b; Pittis and Gabaldón, 2016).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation about gene origins.

claim: Claims concerning differential loss of genes in extant archaea are at odds with pangenomes that support a pan-asgard concept.
source: Claims concerning differential loss of genes in extant archaea (Koonin and Yutin, 2014; Eme et al., 2017) are at odds with pangenomes that support a pan-asgard concept (Knopp et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citing conflicting studies on gene loss versus pangenome analyses.

claim: Molecular clock techniques used to estimate timing of gene duplications are error-prone.
source: The estimated timing of gene duplications that depend on molecular clock techniques that are error-prone (Graur and Martin, 2004; Rodríguez-Trelles et al., 2001; Tiley et al., 2020) with respect to the origins of cellular complexity are also debated (Tria et al., 2021; Vosseberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited critiques of molecular clock methods.

claim: A study using relative branch lengths concluded that mitochondrial metabolism and the ER in eukaryogenesis ensued the origin of the nucleus.
source: A reliance purely on relative branch lengths concluded that mitochondrial metabolism and the ER in eukaryogenesis ensued the origin of the nucleus (Pittis and Gabaldón, 2016).
evidence: This describes the conclusion of a cited study.

claim: The method used by Pittis and Gabaldón (2016) has been questioned.
source: The method used has been questioned (Martin et al., 2017a), and the use of unspecific COG (cluster of orthologous genes) annotations in the study is problematic.
evidence: This is supported by a cited critique of the methodology.

claim: Proteins of the nuclear pore complex were not identified or discussed in the Pittis and Gabaldón (2016) study.
source: Proteins of the nuclear pore complex, of which there are about three dozen (Raices and D'Angelo, 2012), were not identified or discussed, nor was the fact that the nucleus is a specialized compartment of the ER from which it forms during cell division (Anderson and Hetzer, 2008).
evidence: This is a critique of what was missing from a cited study, with supporting citations for the facts mentioned.

claim: The nucleus is a specialized compartment of the ER from which it forms during cell division.
source: Proteins of the nuclear pore complex, of which there are about three dozen (Raices and D'Angelo, 2012), were not identified or discussed, nor was the fact that the nucleus is a specialized compartment of the ER from which it forms during cell division (Anderson and Hetzer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on nuclear formation.

claim: Substitution rates vary substantially across species.
source: Substitution rates that challenge molecular clock studies vary substantially across species (Baer et al., 2007; Halligan and Keightley, 2009) and the functional unit a protein is associated with (Hartwell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on substitution rates.

claim: Thousands of new protein families emerged at eukaryote origin.
source: Considering that thousands of new protein families emerged at eukaryote origin that fall into such categories (Preisner et al., 2018) further highlights the caution with which we need to digest molecular clock studies on eukaryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on protein family emergence.

claim: Seventy percent or more protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits are specific to eukaryotes.
source: Seventy percent or more protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits (such as cell cycle, meiosis, autophagy, nucleus) are specific to eukaryotes, 10–15% (e.g. kinases) are universal across all domains of life, 10–15% are bacterial (e.g. aminopeptidases, mTOR interacting proteins, glycosyltransferases), and a small fraction appear to originate from archaea (DNA licensing proteins of cell cycle, ARG GTPases, N-glycan biosynthesis).
evidence: This is based on analysis of protein family distribution described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: 10-15% of protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits are universal across all domains of life.
source: Seventy percent or more protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits (such as cell cycle, meiosis, autophagy, nucleus) are specific to eukaryotes, 10–15% (e.g. kinases) are universal across all domains of life, 10–15% are bacterial (e.g. aminopeptidases, mTOR interacting proteins, glycosyltransferases), and a small fraction appear to originate from archaea (DNA licensing proteins of cell cycle, ARG GTPases, N-glycan biosynthesis).
evidence: This is based on analysis of protein family distribution described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: 10-15% of protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits are bacterial.
source: Seventy percent or more protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits (such as cell cycle, meiosis, autophagy, nucleus) are specific to eukaryotes, 10–15% (e.g. kinases) are universal across all domains of life, 10–15% are bacterial (e.g. aminopeptidases, mTOR interacting proteins, glycosyltransferases), and a small fraction appear to originate from archaea (DNA licensing proteins of cell cycle, ARG GTPases, N-glycan biosynthesis).
evidence: This is based on analysis of protein family distribution described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: A small fraction of protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits appear to originate from archaea.
source: Seventy percent or more protein families involved in major eukaryotic traits (such as cell cycle, meiosis, autophagy, nucleus) are specific to eukaryotes, 10–15% (e.g. kinases) are universal across all domains of life, 10–15% are bacterial (e.g. aminopeptidases, mTOR interacting proteins, glycosyltransferases), and a small fraction appear to originate from archaea (DNA licensing proteins of cell cycle, ARG GTPases, N-glycan biosynthesis).
evidence: This is based on analysis of protein family distribution described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of protein families involved in eukaryotic cellular complexity are absent across the entire realm of prokaryotic diversity.
source: The distribution of protein families across prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Figure 2) confirms that eukaryotes acquired genes from bacterial or archaeal sources and co-opted them to suit new eukaryotic traits evolving in the FECA to LECA transition, but the majority of protein families involved in eukaryotic cellular complexity are absent across the entire realm of prokaryotic diversity (Brunk and Martin, 2019; Dell et al., 2010; Knopp et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Lombard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and cited studies.

claim: HGT falls short at explaining the pro- to eukaryote transition with respect to the origin of thousands of eukaryote-unique gene families.
source: Hence, HGT falls short at explaining the pro- to eukaryote transition with respect to the origin of thousands of eukaryote-unique gene families and a reason for their positive selection in the absence of an endosymbiont.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of protein families and the need for selective pressure.

claim: Endosymbiotic partners bring along thousands of genes and many were integrated into the host genome.
source: Beyond question, HGT fed into eukaryogenesis – after all, the eukaryotic cell is the product of two prokaryotes – but endosymbiotic partners bring along thousands of genes and many were integrated into the host genome (Timmis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on endosymbiotic gene transfer.

claim: Individual ribosomal gene trees from early releases of asgard archaeal metagenomes were incongruent.
source: For incomplete and contaminated metagenomes (including early releases of asgard archaeal ones), the individual ribosomal gene trees were incongruent (Garg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited analysis of metagenome quality.

claim: The presence of glycerol-3-phosphate lipids in asgard archaea was claimed based on predicted presence of enzymes involved in the synthesis of ester-linked fatty acids.
source: For instance, the presence of glycerol-3-phosphate lipids in asgard archaea was claimed (with far-reaching implications on the lipid transition during eukaryogenesis) based on the predicted presence of enzymes involved in the synthesis of ester-linked fatty acids (Villanueva et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a claim made in a cited study.

claim: No evidence of glycerol-3-phosphate lipids was found in the biochemical analysis of cultured Prometheoarchaeon.
source: No evidence of such lipids, however, was found in the biochemical analysis of a cultured asgard archaeon (Imachi et al., 2020) and the presence of the set of required enzymes in asgard archaea has yet to be identified.
evidence: This is based on biochemical analysis reported in the cited study.

claim: Phylogenetic trees are hypotheses on the evolutionary relationship between organisms and not an observation in itself.
source: It is critical to remember that phylogenetic trees are hypotheses on the evolutionary relationship between organisms and not an observation on itself (Hennig, 2000).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of phylogenetics supported by citation.

claim: Endosymbiosis adds a massive horizontal component to evolution that is still subject to the basic selection and fixation process.
source: Endosymbiosis adds a massive horizontal component to evolution that is, however, still subject to the basic selection and fixation process.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of endosymbiotic evolution.

claim: While the emergence of eukaryotic traits was gradual, the selective pressure that demanded their emergence was more radical.
source: In other words, while the emergence of eukaryotic traits was gradual, the selective pressure that demanded their emergence was more radical.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the evolutionary process.

claim: Microbial syntrophy is the norm.
source: Microbial syntrophy is the norm and so is the selective pressure to optimize it.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of microbial ecology.

claim: Intermediate cell types are not observed among the many syntrophic prokaryotes studied.
source: Why are intermediate cell types not observed among the many syntrophic prokaryotes studied, if it was not for the lack of an endosymbiotic event?
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of intermediate forms in prokaryotes.

claim: Glycosyltransferases are promiscuous enzymes and it has been suggested they are separated through ER-Golgi compartmentalization for that reason.
source: Glycosyltransferases are promiscuous enzymes and it has been suggested they are separated through ER-Golgi compartmentalization for that reason (Biswas and Thattai, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: N- and O-glycosylation are ubiquitous in eukaryotic cells, but not so in prokaryotes.
source: N- and O-glycosylation are ubiquitous in eukaryotic cells, but not so in prokaryotes.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of glycosylation patterns.

claim: Eukaryotic N-glycosylation is likely derived from the archaeal ancestor.
source: Eukaryotic N-glycosylation is likely derived from the archaeal ancestor, while O-glycosylation is more prevalent among bacteria (Abu-Qarn et al., 2008; Dell et al., 2010; Jarrell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on glycosylation evolution.

claim: O-glycosylation is more prevalent among bacteria.
source: Eukaryotic N-glycosylation is likely derived from the archaeal ancestor, while O-glycosylation is more prevalent among bacteria (Abu-Qarn et al., 2008; Dell et al., 2010; Jarrell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on glycosylation patterns.

claim: If each glycosylation pathway stems from one of the prokaryotic partners, natural selection would foster a spatial separation only upon and not prior to endosymbiosis.
source: Hence, if each pathway stems from one of the prokaryotic partners, natural selection would foster a spatial separation only upon and not prior to endosymbiosis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the timing of compartmentalization based on the origins of glycosylation pathways.

claim: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space share notable homologies including calcium storage.
source: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space (the former bacterial periplasm) share notable homologies. This includes calcium storage (Dominguez, 2004; Raffaello et al., 2016), disulfide relay systems (Backes et al., 2019), and redox balance (Cardenas-Rodriguez and Tokatlidis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on ER and mitochondrial biochemistry.

claim: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space share notable homologies including disulfide relay systems.
source: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space (the former bacterial periplasm) share notable homologies. This includes calcium storage (Dominguez, 2004; Raffaello et al., 2016), disulfide relay systems (Backes et al., 2019), and redox balance (Cardenas-Rodriguez and Tokatlidis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on ER and mitochondrial biochemistry.

claim: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space share notable homologies including redox balance.
source: The ER lumen and mitochondrial intramembrane space (the former bacterial periplasm) share notable homologies. This includes calcium storage (Dominguez, 2004; Raffaello et al., 2016), disulfide relay systems (Backes et al., 2019), and redox balance (Cardenas-Rodriguez and Tokatlidis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on ER and mitochondrial biochemistry.

claim: The contact sites of the ER and mitochondrion are cornerstones for the synthesis and regulation of lipids and a plethora of cellular roles.
source: The contact sites of the ER and mitochondrion are cornerstones for the synthesis and regulation of lipids and a plethora of cellular roles (Booth et al., 2016; Flis and Daum, 2013; Friedman et al., 2011; Hamasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on ER-mitochondrial contact sites.

claim: The ER could have stemmed from mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs).
source: This could be a consequence of the ER stemming from mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs) (Gould et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: MDVs could have provided the necessary endomembrane material for compartmentalization.
source: MDVs could have provided the necessary endomembrane material for compartmentalization and remain the most plausible source for the lipid transition from ether-linked, archaeal head groups to ester-linked (bacterial) eukaryotic head groups.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the role of MDVs in eukaryogenesis.

claim: MDVs remain the most plausible source for the lipid transition from ether-linked, archaeal head groups to ester-linked (bacterial) eukaryotic head groups.
source: MDVs could have provided the necessary endomembrane material for compartmentalization and remain the most plausible source for the lipid transition from ether-linked, archaeal head groups to ester-linked (bacterial) eukaryotic head groups.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of lipid transition.

claim: MDVs exist and play a role in eukaryotic biology.
source: Much on the origin of the endomembrane system remains a speculation, but not so the existence of MDVs, their role in eukaryotic biology, and how they induce compartment formation (Schuler et al., 2021; Sugiura et al., 2017; Sugiura et al., 2014; Yamashita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on MDVs.

claim: MDVs induce compartment formation.
source: Much on the origin of the endomembrane system remains a speculation, but not so the existence of MDVs, their role in eukaryotic biology, and how they induce compartment formation (Schuler et al., 2021; Sugiura et al., 2017; Sugiura et al., 2014; Yamashita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on MDVs.

claim: Vesicle secretion from the plasma membrane into the environment is a common trait of all cells.
source: Vesicle secretion from the plasma membrane into the environment is a common trait of all cells.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of cell biology.

claim: Eukaryotes can internalize membrane vesicles of various sizes using different molecular machineries.
source: Unique to eukaryotes are the many ways with which they can internalize membrane vesicles of various sizes, ranging from clathrin-mediated endocytosis (~100 nm) to phagocytosis (>750 nm), using different molecular machineries.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of eukaryotic cell biology.

claim: All compartments that define the endomembrane system are conserved across eukaryotes and absent in prokaryotes.
source: All compartments that define the endomembrane system – with the ER at its core – as well as the majority of regulatory and structural proteins are conserved across eukaryotes and absent in prokaryotes (Klinger et al., 2016; Kontou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited comparative studies.

claim: The nucleus is a distinctive extension of the ER and forms from the latter after mitosis.
source: The nucleus is a distinctive extension of the ER and forms from the latter after mitosis (Anderson and Hetzer, 2008) using homologs of ESRCT complex (Olmos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on nuclear formation.

claim: The nucleus forms using homologs of ESCRT complex.
source: The nucleus is a distinctive extension of the ER and forms from the latter after mitosis (Anderson and Hetzer, 2008) using homologs of ESRCT complex (Olmos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on nuclear formation mechanisms.

claim: The nucleus separates transcription from translation and is the site of pre-ribosome assembly.
source: It separates transcription from translation and is the site of pre-ribosome assembly (Peña et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of nuclear function, with citation for ribosome assembly.

claim: A plausible selection for the nucleus could have been imposed by the transfer of group II introns from the endosymbiont that drove the origin of eukaryotic splicing.
source: A plausible selection could have been imposed by the transfer of group II introns from the endosymbiont that drove the origin of eukaryotic splicing and need for separating transcription slowed by the spliceosome from fast translation (Martin and Koonin, 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: Mitochondria-early scenarios provide both the problem (group II introns that need to be spliced) and the solution (MDVs that might have given rise to the ER).
source: Mitochondria-early scenarios provide both the problem (group II introns that need to be spliced) and the solution (MDVs that might have given rise to the ER) (Gould et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument from a cited study.

claim: The prokaryotic solution to prevent mutational overload through Muller's ratchet is HGT.
source: The prokaryotic solution to prevent mutational overload through Muller's ratchet is HGT (Muller, 1964).
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary theory with citation.

claim: The nucleus renders the eukaryotic cytoplasm almost sterile of DNA, preventing HGT.
source: The nucleus renders the eukaryotic cytoplasm almost sterile of DNA (preventing HGT), wherein it plays a regulatory immune function (Abe et al., 2019; Paludan and Bowie, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on nuclear function in immunity.

claim: The eukaryotic solution to Muller's ratchet was ploidy, multinucleated cells and reciprocal recombination through meiosis.
source: The eukaryotic solution was ploidy, multinucleated cells and reciprocal recombination through meiosis (Garg and Martin, 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: A multinucleated state is readily achieved by decoupling nuclear from cell division, a mechanism commonly observed in prokaryotes.
source: A multinucleated state is readily achieved by decoupling nuclear from cell division, a mechanism commonly observed in prokaryotes wherein the DNA replicates independently of the cell before portioning into daughter cells (Haeusser and Levin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on prokaryotic cell division.

claim: The syncytial theory posits that by virtue of multinucleated cells within a singular archaeal host, multiplying bacterial symbionts are free to lose genes via endosymbiotic gene transfer to the multiple copies of the host nucleus.
source: The syncytial theory for eukaryotic origin (Garg and Martin, 2016) posits that by virtue of multinucleated cells within a singular archaeal host, multiplying bacterial symbionts are free to lose genes via endosymbiotic gene transfer to the multiple copies of the host nucleus/nuclear material in the cytoplasm to explore various configurations under the constant onslaught of group II introns, yet retaining fitness by compensating viable mRNA in-trans within the same shared cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a detailed explanation of a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: The syncytial model explains how homologous recombination was necessary to maintain viable copies of undisrupted genes while simultaneously maintaining the presence of bacterial transferred genes.
source: The explanatory power of this model is twofold: (i) it explains how homologous recombination – which subsequently evolved to meiosis as we understand it today – was necessary to maintain viable copies of undisrupted genes, while simultaneously maintaining the presence of bacterial transferred genes, and (ii), it explains the monophyly of eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an explanation of the theoretical implications of the syncytial model.

claim: The syncytial model explains the monophyly of eukaryotes.
source: The explanatory power of this model is twofold: (i) it explains how homologous recombination – which subsequently evolved to meiosis as we understand it today – was necessary to maintain viable copies of undisrupted genes, while simultaneously maintaining the presence of bacterial transferred genes, and (ii), it explains the monophyly of eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an explanation of the theoretical implications of the syncytial model.

claim: Meiosis is ancient, ubiquitous, and the central process that imparts an advantage to sex in eukaryotes.
source: Meiosis in itself is ancient, ubiquitous, and the central process that imparts an advantage to sex in eukaryotes (Colnaghi et al., 2022; Colnaghi et al., 2020; Malik et al., 2008; Speijer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on meiosis evolution.

claim: Several theories place mito-nuclear interactions, heteroplasmy, and mitochondrial ROS as drivers of eukaryotic sex.
source: Several theories place mito-nuclear interactions, heteroplasmy, and mitochondrial ROS as drivers of eukaryotic sex (Colnaghi et al., 2020; Hörandl and Speijer, 2018; Radzvilavicius and Blackstone, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited theoretical studies.

claim: HGT alone was insufficient for LECA to escape Muller's ratchet in the absence of homologous recombination.
source: HGT alone was insufficient for LECA to escape Mullers ratchet in the absence of homologous recombination (Colnaghi et al., 2022), when considering expanding genome size and repeat sequence frequency.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on the limitations of HGT.

claim: Everything points to an origin of sex and meiosis necessitated by the presence of mitochondria.
source: Everything points to an origin of sex and meiosis necessitated by the presence of mitochondria.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple lines of evidence discussed in the text.

claim: The majority of enzymes of peroxisomal beta-oxidation are of alphaproteobacterial origin.
source: The majority of enzymes of peroxisomal beta-oxidation are of alphaproteobacterial origin (Bolte et al., 2015) and peroxisomes might have evolved to compartmentalize ROS-producing beta-oxidation and protect the mitochondrial genome (Speijer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited phylogenetic study.

claim: Peroxisomes might have evolved to compartmentalize ROS-producing beta-oxidation and protect the mitochondrial genome.
source: The majority of enzymes of peroxisomal beta-oxidation are of alphaproteobacterial origin (Bolte et al., 2015) and peroxisomes might have evolved to compartmentalize ROS-producing beta-oxidation and protect the mitochondrial genome (Speijer, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: De novo biosynthesis of peroxisomes involves MDVs with integrated Pex3 and Pex14 that fuse with ER-derived vesicles containing Pex16.
source: De novo biosynthesis of peroxisomes involves MDVs with integrated Pex3 and Pex14 that fuse with ER-derived vesicles containing Pex16 (Sugiura et al., 2017), and the compartment for beta-oxidation appears absent in species lacking respiring mitochondria (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on peroxisome biogenesis.

claim: The compartment for beta-oxidation appears absent in species lacking respiring mitochondria.
source: De novo biosynthesis of peroxisomes involves MDVs with integrated Pex3 and Pex14 that fuse with ER-derived vesicles containing Pex16 (Sugiura et al., 2017), and the compartment for beta-oxidation appears absent in species lacking respiring mitochondria (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited comparative study.

claim: Cytosolic protein homeostasis in prokaryotes is performed by proteases and proteasomes, which are common to both archaea and bacteria.
source: Cytosolic protein homeostasis in prokaryotes is performed by proteases and proteasomes, which are common to both archaea and bacteria.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of prokaryotic protein degradation.

claim: Defective membrane proteins and membranes in prokaryotes are shed by mechanisms similar to bacterial outer membrane vesicle secretion.
source: Defective membrane proteins and membranes are shed by mechanisms similar to bacterial outer membrane vesicle secretion (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on bacterial vesicle secretion.

claim: Eukaryotes utilize membrane-bound compartments in the form of autophagosomes for recycling membranes including their proteins.
source: Eukaryotes utilize membrane-bound compartments in the form of autophagosomes, also for recycling membranes including their proteins (Nakatogawa, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited review on autophagy.

claim: Mitophagy removes damaged mitochondria and is initiated by ER-mitochondrial contact sites.
source: Mitophagy removes damaged mitochondria and is initiated by ER-mitochondrial contact sites (Hamasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on mitophagy mechanisms.

claim: Autophagy is a trait needed in the presence of large intracellular compartments and the occasional yet inevitable breakdown of organelles that require immediate containment.
source: It is a trait needed in the presence of large intracellular compartments and the occasional yet inevitable breakdown of organelles that require immediate containment (Anding and Baehrecke, 2017).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation supported by a cited study.

claim: The eukaryotic cell cycle is a series of choreographed steps that leads to the correct portioning of genetic material, endomembrane, and organelles to both daughter cells.
source: The eukaryotic cell cycle is a series of choreographed steps that leads to the correct portioning of genetic material, endomembrane, and organelles to both daughter cells (Harashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of the cell cycle with citation.

claim: The presence of a nuclear compartment and an endosymbiont are incompatible with binary fission in the absence of orchestrated replication and organelle and compartment division, and cytokinesis.
source: The presence of a nuclear compartment and an endosymbiont are incompatible with binary fission in the absence of orchestrated replication and organelle and compartment division, and cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for eukaryotic cell division.

claim: In prokaryotes the nuclear material (genome) replicates independently of cell division.
source: As mentioned in the previous section, in prokaryotes the nuclear material (genome) replicates independently of cell division, which would have facilitated the formation of syncytial populations (Haeusser and Levin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on prokaryotic cell division.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolism started playing a significant role in controlling cell division during eukaryogenesis.
source: During this time, however, we speculate that mitochondrial metabolism started playing a more significant role in controlling cell division, given the role of nutrient availability in coordination of cell division.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The G1 phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle results in the mitochondria as the master regulator for S/G2 progression.
source: The G1 phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle results in the mitochondria as the master regulator for S/G2 progression (Antico Arciuch et al., 2012; Mitra et al., 2009), suggestive of a deep link between mitochondria and the cell cycle and one that would have been difficult to integrate into a pre-existing one.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on mitochondrial regulation of the cell cycle.

claim: Eukaryotic cell division employs the use of ESCRT homologs and actin in contrast to bacterial division mechanisms involving FtsZs.
source: Eukaryotic cell division employs the use of ESCRT homologs and actin in contrast to bacterial division mechanisms involving FtsZs from which also tubulin evolved (Christ et al., 2016; Goliand et al., 2014; Stoten and Carlton, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cell division mechanisms.

claim: Tubulin evolved from FtsZs.
source: Eukaryotic cell division employs the use of ESCRT homologs and actin in contrast to bacterial division mechanisms involving FtsZs from which also tubulin evolved (Christ et al., 2016; Goliand et al., 2014; Stoten and Carlton, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited evolutionary studies.

claim: Eukaryotic cell division evolved an independent pathway involving ESCRT proteins consistent with their role in archaeal cell division.
source: This suggests the evolution of an independent pathway for cell division involving ESCRT proteins consistent with their role in archaeal cell division (Tarrason Risa et al., 2020), one that was based on outer membrane vesicle secretion, but this time packaging mitochondria and the nucleus/genetic material, the latter similar to a role of prokaryotic OMVs (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited studies on ESCRT function.

claim: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton rests on three main pillars: actin and associated proteins, tubulin and associated proteins, and intermediate filament proteins.
source: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton rests on three main pillars: (i) actin and associated proteins, (ii) tubulin and associated proteins, and (iii) the utterly diverse intermediate filament (IF) proteins.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of cytoskeletal organization.

claim: Components of each cytoskeletal pillar can be found in archaea and bacteria alike.
source: Components of each pillar, sometimes also in combination, can be found in archaea and bacteria alike (Duggin et al., 2015; Larsen et al., 2007; Preisner et al., 2018; van den Ent et al., 2001; Wickstead and Gull, 2011; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited comparative studies.

claim: The intricate combination and universal presence of all three cytoskeletal pillars and the dynamic nature which they are used in eukaryotes is characteristic.
source: As with many things in eukaryogenesis, it is the intricate combination and universal presence of all three cytoskeletal pillars and the dynamic nature which they are used in eukaryotes that is characteristic.
evidence: This is an observation about what distinguishes eukaryotic cytoskeletons.

claim: Many protists can rapidly switch between actin-based gliding and tubulin-based flagella-driven swimming, likely also a feature of the LECA.
source: The latter is best demonstrated by the rapid switch in motility between actin-based gliding and tubulin-based flagella-driven swimming in many protists, likely also a feature of the LECA (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010; Kusdian et al., 2013; Preisner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on protist motility.

claim: Basic cytoskeletal components were derived from the host cell, such as gelsolin-regulated actin filaments.
source: Basic components were derived from the host cell, such as gelsolin-regulated actin filaments (Akıl et al., 2020) and evolution co-opted such mechanisms en route to LECA.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on actin regulation.

claim: With expanding cell size, increased intracellular complexity and the need of an orchestrated cell cycle, the selection for a dynamic but simultaneously in parts rigid cytoskeleton increased.
source: It is conceivable that with expanding cell size, increased intracellular complexity and the need of an orchestrated cell cycle, the selection for a dynamic but simultaneously in parts rigid cytoskeleton increased, which triggered the expansion of the IF protein family required for mechanical support, and the origin of additional accessory proteins and regulatory mechanisms that are absent in prokaryotes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the selective pressures driving cytoskeletal evolution.

claim: Asgard archaea underpin the syntrophic origin of eukaryotes involving two prokaryotic partners.
source: The identification and subsequent characterizations of asgard archaea have done the following for eukaryogenesis: (i) They underpin the syntrophic origin of eukaryotes involving two prokaryotic partners and (ii) provide support for a 2D tree of life (i.e. two domains of life, bacteria and archaea, evolved from the origin of life and eukaryotes emerged from within archaea after endosymbiosis of an alphaproteobacterial partner).
evidence: This is a synthesis of what asgard archaea discoveries have contributed to understanding eukaryogenesis.

claim: Asgard archaea provide support for a 2D tree of life.
source: The identification and subsequent characterizations of asgard archaea have done the following for eukaryogenesis: (i) They underpin the syntrophic origin of eukaryotes involving two prokaryotic partners and (ii) provide support for a 2D tree of life (i.e. two domains of life, bacteria and archaea, evolved from the origin of life and eukaryotes emerged from within archaea after endosymbiosis of an alphaproteobacterial partner).
evidence: This is a synthesis of what asgard archaea discoveries have contributed to understanding the tree of life.

claim: Asgard archaea provide no evidence for the presence of bacterial-type ester-linked lipids.
source: (iii) They provide no evidence for the presence of bacterial-type ester-linked lipids in asgard archaea, (iv) reject a complex archaeal ancestor necessary to explain the patchy distribution of eukaryogenesis-relevant gene families (Wu et al., 2022), and (v) show that the asgard archaeal set of genes before unique to eukaryotes closes the gap to the number of gene families encoded by eukaryotes by only 0.3% (Knopp et al., 2021) or less (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on biochemical analysis of cultured asgard archaea.

claim: Asgard archaea reject a complex archaeal ancestor necessary to explain the patchy distribution of eukaryogenesis-relevant gene families.
source: (iii) They provide no evidence for the presence of bacterial-type ester-linked lipids in asgard archaea, (iv) reject a complex archaeal ancestor necessary to explain the patchy distribution of eukaryogenesis-relevant gene families (Wu et al., 2022), and (v) show that the asgard archaeal set of genes before unique to eukaryotes closes the gap to the number of gene families encoded by eukaryotes by only 0.3% (Knopp et al., 2021) or less (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited phylogenomic study.

claim: The asgard archaeal set of genes unique to eukaryotes closes the gap to the number of gene families encoded by eukaryotes by only 0.3% or less.
source: (iii) They provide no evidence for the presence of bacterial-type ester-linked lipids in asgard archaea, (iv) reject a complex archaeal ancestor necessary to explain the patchy distribution of eukaryogenesis-relevant gene families (Wu et al., 2022), and (v) show that the asgard archaeal set of genes before unique to eukaryotes closes the gap to the number of gene families encoded by eukaryotes by only 0.3% (Knopp et al., 2021) or less (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited pangenome analyses.

claim: Syntrophy was a key ecological parameter in eukaryogenesis.
source: Considering syntrophy as a key ecological parameter in eukaryogenesis was an early notion that has stood the test of time (Imachi et al., 2020; López-García and Moreira, 2020; López-García and Moreira, 2019; Sousa et al., 2016; Spang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on eukaryogenesis.

claim: Eukaryogenesis likely occurred within a microbial mat, where multiple species thrive in close proximity and exchange substrates such as H2/electrons under limited or no oxygen.
source: Ever since, observations from the field of microbial ecology, genomics, and geology continue to encourage us to picture eukaryogenesis to have occurred within a microbial mat, where multiple species thrive in close proximity and ample syntrophies exchanging substrates such as H2/electrons under limited or no oxygen (López-García and Moreira, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited ecological and geological studies.

claim: Recent advances in geochemistry added new support to the proposal that eukaryogenesis occurred in anoxic niches with a preferred shift towards aerobic metabolism being a secondarily derived state.
source: Recent advances in geochemistry added new support to the proposal that eukaryogenesis occurred in anoxic niches with a preferred shift towards aerobic metabolism being a secondarily derived state (Mills et al., 2022) and so do the culturing conditions of Prometheoarchaeon (Imachi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited geochemical and culturing studies.

claim: Prokaryotic consortia can source genes through HGT from pangenomes of other bacteria and archaea and the virosphere.
source: Such prokaryotic consortia can source genes through HGT from pangenomes of other bacteria and (asgard) archaea and the virosphere that also contributed to the birth of the eukaryotic genome (Spang et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited genomic studies.

claim: Most eukaryotic protein families evolved during the FECA to LECA transition.
source: Evidently, however, most eukaryotic protein families evolved during the FECA to LECA transition and selective pressures due to endosymbiosis were likely key.
evidence: This is an inference based on protein family distribution data.

claim: Physiological and phylogenomic studies support a mitochondria-early scenario.
source: To conclude, physiological and phylogenomic studies support a mitochondria-early scenario and so does cell biology (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple lines of evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Claiming mitochondria were of little importance in eukaryogenesis contradicts the simultaneous claim that intermediates lacking mitochondria all went extinct.
source: Claiming mitochondria were of little importance in eukaryogenesis contradicts the simultaneous claim that intermediates lacking mitochondria all went extinct – an oxymoron that suggests that the mitochondrial endosymbiont contributed little in the FECA to LECA transition, while its presence was vital for the survival of FECA during eukaryogenesis.
evidence: This is a logical critique of contradictory positions in the field.

claim: In eukaryogenesis we are dealing with at least a 10 times increase in cell diameter.
source: In eukaryogenesis we are dealing with at least a 10 times increase in cell diameter, with known consequences regarding cell volume, morphology, and molecular diffusion limits among other factors (Young, 2006).
evidence: This is based on comparative cell size data with citation.

claim: Engulfing a proteobacterium with a surface area of 10 µm2 requires 10 times the surface area of the asgard archaeon Prometheoarchaeon.
source: Engulfing a proteobacterium with a surface area of 10 µm2 requires 10 times the surface area of the asgard archaeon Prometheoarchaeon.
evidence: This is a calculation based on cell size measurements.

claim: For a typical protist, engulfing a proteobacterium is only 1% of its surface area.
source: For a typical protist it is only 1% of its surface area.
evidence: This is a calculation based on cell size measurements.

claim: An observed tubular protrusion in Prometheoarchaeon requires 12% of cytoplasm for a 50% increase in surface area interacting with syntrophic partners.
source: Putting scales on a recent model, the entangle-engulf-endogenize mode (Imachi et al., 2020) brings forth details worthy considering: an observed tubular protrusion requires 12% of cytoplasm for a 50% increase in surface area interacting with syntrophic partners (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a calculation based on measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: Four to six protrusions approximately result in the doubling of cytosolic volume in Prometheoarchaeon.
source: Four to six protrusions approximately result in the doubling of cytosolic volume, maybe explaining why Prometheoarchaeon has not been observed to produce more than six protrusion per cell.
evidence: This is a calculation and inference based on cell geometry.

claim: The surface area of a protrusion is 3% that of a proteobacterium.
source: Such protrusions might have been relevant for the uptake of the symbiont, but the surface area of such a protrusion is 3% that of a proteobacterium.
evidence: This is a calculation based on cell size measurements.

claim: Entangling a proteobacterium entirely would take at minimum 50 protrusions.
source: Entangling a proteobacterium entirely would take at minimum 50 protrusions, the cost of which is six times the cytoplasmic volume and not considering the multitude of proteins needed for recognition, surface attachment, and the processes thereof.
evidence: This is a calculation based on surface area requirements.

claim: Across eukaryotes, an increase in cell size (1000–10,000 times) and morphological complexity is common, matched by a comparable increase in genome size.
source: Across eukaryotes, an increase in cell size (1000–10,000 times) and morphological complexity is common, matched by a comparable increase in genome size.
evidence: This is based on comparative data across eukaryotes.

claim: The upper end of bacterial genomes is 15 Mb.
source: The upper end of bacterial genomes is 15 Mb (Land et al., 2015), that of (haploid) eukaryote is around 130 Bb (Pellicer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited genomic studies.

claim: The upper end of haploid eukaryotic genomes is around 130 Gb.
source: The upper end of bacterial genomes is 15 Mb (Land et al., 2015), that of (haploid) eukaryote is around 130 Bb (Pellicer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a cited genomic study.

claim: In prokaryotes ATP production is limited by the available cell surface.
source: In prokaryotes ATP production is limited by the available cell surface. This limits the replication rate and imposes negative selection on genome expansion (Lane, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited bioenergetic study.

claim: Limited ATP production by cell surface limits the replication rate and imposes negative selection on genome expansion in prokaryotes.
source: In prokaryotes ATP production is limited by the available cell surface. This limits the replication rate and imposes negative selection on genome expansion (Lane, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited bioenergetic study.

claim: In mitochondria powered eukaryotes, energetic efficiency increases with cell size.
source: Conversely, in mitochondria powered eukaryotes, energetic efficiency increases with cell size (Hochachka et al., 2003; Lane, 2007), imposing a positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by cited bioenergetic studies.

claim: Increased cell size in eukaryotes means increased DNA content to maintain the karyoplasmic ratio.
source: Increased cell size in eukaryotes means increased DNA content to maintain the karyoplasmic ratio (Cavalier-Smith, 2005; Cavalier-Smith, 1985), which is positively selected for (Lane, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cell size and genome size relationships.

claim: Endosymbiosis provided an influx of endosymbiotic genes and membrane material.
source: Endosymbiosis provided an influx of endosymbiotic genes and membrane material.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of endosymbiosis.

claim: Constant fusion of endosymbiont-derived vesicles with the archaeal host provided a mechanism for the lipid shift and compartment origin.
source: Constant fusion of endosymbiont-derived vesicles with the archaeal host provided a mechanism for the lipid shift and compartment origin (Gould et al., 2016), which might have fostered an increase in cell size.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: Integration of endosymbiotic DNA provided one early mechanism for why the genome size increased.
source: Integration of endosymbiotic DNA provided one early mechanism for why the genome size increased, together with duplication events (Kelly, 2021; Tria et al., 2021; Van de Peer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on genome evolution.

claim: The ongoing concentration of ATP synthesis to mitochondria imposed positive selection on cell size.
source: The ongoing concentration of ATP synthesis to mitochondria imposed positive selection on cell size, which allowed for a further increase in genome size.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about bioenergetic constraints on evolution.

claim: A feed-forward process of increased cell size stipulating increased genome size and vice versa commenced that was supported by an emerging endomembrane system.
source: A feed-forward process of increased cell size stipulating increased genome size and vice versa commenced that was supported by an emerging endomembrane system and intracellular transport that counteracted the molecular diffusion limit (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary dynamics during eukaryogenesis, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The feed-forward process provided ground for new combinations of genes to emerge and be expressed.
source: It provided ground for new combinations of genes to emerge and expressed (Lane and Martin, 2010) and increased cell size accommodated experimental expression of new proteins in the cytosol (Dill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited theoretical studies.

claim: Increased cell size accommodated experimental expression of new proteins in the cytosol.
source: It provided ground for new combinations of genes to emerge and expressed (Lane and Martin, 2010) and increased cell size accommodated experimental expression of new proteins in the cytosol (Dill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on protein expression constraints.

claim: Most new protein inventions during eukaryogenesis revolve around the endosymbiont.
source: Considering that most of these new inventions revolve around the endosymbiont (Figure 3), suggests it drove the selection for their emergence and fixation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eukaryotes have innovated several folds higher number of protein families than archaea.
source: Eukaryotes have innovated several folds higher number of protein families than archaea as evident from genome (Brueckner and Martin, 2020) and proteome data (Müller et al., 2020) alike, underpinning the complexity across the eukaryotic tree of life.
evidence: This is supported by cited genomic and proteomic studies.

claim: Mutations lack foresight and are more likely to be deleterious than advantageous.
source: Since mutations lack foresight and are more likely to be deleterious than advantageous (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007), inventing new proteins takes a considerable amount of trial and error.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary theory with citation.

claim: Ribosome production and protein biosynthesis consumes the majority of a cell's energy budget.
source: Ribosome production and protein biosynthesis consumes the majority of a cell's energy budget (Harold, 1986; Kafri et al., 2016) and the energy budget of trial and error would be orders of magnitude higher.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on cellular energetics.

claim: Mitochondria were key by providing eukaryogenesis with an energetic freedom that supported an unparalleled level of innovative protein evolution and expression.
source: Mitochondria were key by providing eukaryogenesis with an energetic freedom that supported this unparalleled level of innovative protein evolution and expression (Lane and Martin, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: The bioenergetic contribution of mitochondria has been challenged but not disproven.
source: While challenged (Lynch and Marinov, 2017; Schavemaker and Muñoz-Gómez, 2022), we do not see it disproven (Gerlitz et al., 2018; Lane, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of debate in the field with citations.

claim: Calculations questioning the bioenergetic contribution of mitochondria do not account for the cost of evolving novel proteins.
source: Calculations questioning the bioenergetic contribution of mitochondria do not account for the cost of evolving novel proteins.
evidence: This is a critique of alternative calculations.

claim: The acquisition of a respiratory electron transport chain through excessive HGT does not make a cell complex.
source: The acquisition of a respiratory electron transport chain through excessive HGT does not make a cell complex ( Nelson-Sathi et al., 2012), because the location of the bioenergetic membrane matters.
evidence: This is supported by a cited case study of haloarchaea.

claim: The ratio of bioenergetic membrane to genome size is high when harbouring an endosymbiont with internalized energetic membranes and a reduced genome.
source: The ratio of bioenergetic membrane (=energy generation) to genome size is high when harbouring an endosymbiont with internalized energetic membranes and a reduced genome (Lane and Martin, 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument from a cited study.

claim: A bioenergetic plasma membrane is incompatible with phagocytosis.
source: Also, a bioenergetic plasma membrane is incompatible with phagocytosis and the internalization of the bioenergetic membrane was a prerequisite to evolve phagocytosis (Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument from a cited study.

claim: The internalization of the bioenergetic membrane was a prerequisite to evolve phagocytosis.
source: Also, a bioenergetic plasma membrane is incompatible with phagocytosis and the internalization of the bioenergetic membrane was a prerequisite to evolve phagocytosis (Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument from a cited study.

claim: Eukaryotes that maintain complexity in the absence of respiring mitochondria are either parasites or commensals of eukaryotes and are energetically dependent on canonical mitochondria.
source: Eukaryotes that maintain complexity in the absence of respiring mitochondria has prompted some to question the importance of mitochondria and a surplus of ATP at eukaryote origin (Hampl et al., 2019), while missing a critical detail: the examples listed stem from species that are either parasites or commensals of eukaryotes and who are energetically dependent on canonical mitochondria.
evidence: This is a critique of an argument with supporting reasoning.

claim: Monocercomonoides is the only eukaryotic taxon not possessing mitochondria.
source: The same holds true for the only eukaryotic taxon not possessing mitochondria, Monocercomonoides. They secondarily lost mitochondria and can only thrive in the gut of some animals (Karnkowska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on Monocercomonoides.

claim: Monocercomonoides secondarily lost mitochondria and can only thrive in the gut of some animals.
source: The same holds true for the only eukaryotic taxon not possessing mitochondria, Monocercomonoides. They secondarily lost mitochondria and can only thrive in the gut of some animals (Karnkowska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on Monocercomonoides.

claim: The issue is the origin of eukaryote complexity from prokaryotic ancestors, not the maintenance of eukaryotic complexity from eukaryotic ancestors.
source: The issue is the origin of eukaryote complexity from prokaryotic ancestors, not the maintenance of eukaryotic complexity from eukaryotic ancestors.
evidence: This is a clarification of what needs to be explained in eukaryogenesis.

claim: The internalization of energetic membrane provides an optimum for protein innovation.
source: The internalization of energetic membrane – energy production from only 10% of cell volume – decoupled from the genome, as is the case in mitochondria (Fenchel, 2014), provides an optimum for protein innovation and a selection towards a complexity that can maintain a 200 ton blue whale.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by citation.

claim: Endosymbiosis is absent among prokaryotes apart from isolated exceptions.
source: Endosymbiosis is absent among prokaryotes (apart from isolated exceptions) and so is morphological complexity comparable to that of eukaryotes (reviewed in Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is based on a review of prokaryotic biology.

claim: Morphological complexity comparable to that of eukaryotes is absent among prokaryotes.
source: Endosymbiosis is absent among prokaryotes (apart from isolated exceptions) and so is morphological complexity comparable to that of eukaryotes (reviewed in Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is based on a review of prokaryotic biology.

claim: It is unlikely that the endosymbiosis leading into the origin of the eukaryotic domain was the first and only attempt throughout 4 billion years of prokaryotic evolution.
source: It is unlikely that the endosymbiosis leading into the origin of the eukaryotic domain was the first and only attempt throughout now 4 billion years of prokaryotic evolution.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the long history of prokaryotic evolution.

claim: There is a constant influx of endosymbiotic DNA during endosymbiosis.
source: The set of challenges posed by an endosymbiont are generic in nature: (i) there is a constant influx of endosymbiotic DNA which, after integration into the host genome (Allen, 2015; Portugez et al., 2018), is also exposed to an increased accumulation of deleterious mutations (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on endosymbiotic gene transfer.

claim: Endosymbiotic DNA after integration into the host genome is exposed to an increased accumulation of deleterious mutations.
source: The set of challenges posed by an endosymbiont are generic in nature: (i) there is a constant influx of endosymbiotic DNA which, after integration into the host genome (Allen, 2015; Portugez et al., 2018), is also exposed to an increased accumulation of deleterious mutations (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on mutation rates.

claim: The secretion of outer membrane vesicles by the endosymbiont is inevitable.
source: The secretion of outer membrane vesicles by the endosymbiont is inevitable (Deatherage and Cookson, 2012), as well as the removal of irreversibly damaged organelles or the need to supply the endosymbiont with substrate from ions to peptides.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on bacterial vesicle secretion.

claim: A lot of solutions to endosymbiont challenges are associated with compartmentalization.
source: A lot of solutions are associated with compartmentalization and this is a good time to remember that the mitochondrial endosymbiont not only provided the challenges, but maybe also the material to solve some (Gould et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of solutions to endosymbiosis challenges.

claim: The mitochondrial endosymbiont not only provided the challenges, but maybe also the material to solve some.
source: A lot of solutions are associated with compartmentalization and this is a good time to remember that the mitochondrial endosymbiont not only provided the challenges, but maybe also the material to solve some (Gould et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: Any attempts at eukaryogenesis are prone to fail if challenges are not met by solutions that require correct timing.
source: Any attempts at eukaryogenesis are prone to fail, if such challenges are not met by solutions that furthermore require correct timing (Barbrook et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by citation.

claim: An influx of genes via HGT alone does not translate into complexity.
source: An influx of genes via HGT alone does not translate into complexity.
evidence: This is supported by the example of haloarchaea discussed in the text.

claim: Haloarchaea underwent metabolic transformation via a chunk of some 1000 genes of bacterial origin but show no intracellular complexity.
source: Despite the metabolic transformation of haloarchaea via a chunk of some 1000 genes of bacterial origin (Nelson-Sathi et al., 2012) – maybe through a syntrophic partner and failed endosymbiosis – haloarchaea show no intracellular complexity.
evidence: This is based on a cited study of haloarchaea genomics.

claim: While the encounter of the mitochondrial ancestor with an archaeal host occurred by chance, the emergence of a complex cell biology upon endosymbiosis was a necessity.
source: So while the encounter of the mitochondrial ancestor with an archaeal host occurred by chance, the emergence of a complex cell biology upon endosymbiosis was a necessity.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about the nature of eukaryogenesis.

claim: Once a cell biology that can chaperone an endosymbiont is established, additional endosymbionts may follow without noticeable changes to the host.
source: Once a cell biology that can chaperone an endosymbiont is established, however, additional endosymbionts may follow without noticeable changes to the host.
evidence: This is supported by observations of plastid acquisition discussed in the text.

claim: The subsequent acquisition of the plastid added no extra compartments to the heterotrophic host that gave rise to the Archaeplastida.
source: The subsequent acquisition of the plastid added no extra compartments to the heterotrophic host that gave rise to the Archaeplastida, despite adding thousands of cyanobacterial genes to the host genome (Timmis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on plastid evolution.

claim: An independent plastid acquisition by a rhizarian protist added no extra compartments.
source: The same is true for an independent plastid acquisition by a rhizarian protist (Lhee et al., 2019) and likely many other endosymbiont-bearing protists (Husnik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on plastid acquisition.

claim: Since eukaryogenesis, the cellular framework required for housing another prokaryote was in place.
source: Ever since eukaryogenesis, the cellular framework required for housing another prokaryote was in place.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of subsequent endosymbioses.

claim: Many components that evolved to service mitochondria during eukaryogenesis were recycled for the plastid.
source: Some compartments have experienced physiological remodelling, such as the peroxisome (Islinger et al., 2010), but many components that evolved to service mitochondria during eukaryogenesis were recycled for the plastid: dynamins for fission (Fujimoto and Tsutsumi, 2014), redox balance through thioredoxins (Thormählen et al., 2017), and organelle digestion and recycling through the autophagosome (Ishida et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on plastid biology.

claim: In secondary endosymbioses, the acquisition of algae by eukaryotic hosts can lead to the stripping of all eukaryotic compartments of the endosymbionts but add no additional compartment or complexity to the host.
source: One could add secondary endosymbioses, in which the acquisition of algae by eukaryotic hosts can lead to the stripping of all eukaryotic compartments of the endosymbionts (including their mitochondria), but that otherwise add no additional compartment or complexity to the host.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of secondary endosymbiosis.

claim: Morphologically complex life on Earth has a singular origin: eukaryogenesis.
source: Morphologically complex life on Earth has a singular origin: eukaryogenesis.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic evidence of eukaryotic monophyly.

claim: The LECA had evolved all canonical traits that separate prokaryotic from eukaryotic life.
source: The LECA had evolved all canonical traits that we understand separates prokaryotic from eukaryotic life.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomics and cell biology.

claim: Closing the gap between a simple FECA and a complex LECA by presupposing a complex FECA opens an equally wide gap between a simple and a complex archaeal host.
source: Closing the gap between a simple FECA and a complex LECA by presupposing a complex FECA opens an equally wide gap between a simple and a complex archaeal host.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the implications of different models.

claim: Picturing FECA without an endosymbiont offers little explanation for the existence or emergence of eukaryotic traits and the lack thereof in prokaryotes.
source: Picturing FECA without an endosymbiont offers little explanation for the existence or emergence of eukaryotic traits and the lack thereof in prokaryotes (including asgard archaea), apart from the inevitable that all eukaryogenesis models face: the need to script the blueprint of a eukaryotic cell.
evidence: This is a critique of mitochondria-late models.

claim: For 4 billion years, prokaryotes have overall remained the same in terms of cellular complexity with some rare exceptions having evolved a single compartment type.
source: For 4 billion years, prokaryotes have overall remained the same in terms of cellular complexity with some rare exceptions having evolved a single compartment type, but nothing vaguely similar to the conserved nature of the eukaryotic endomembrane system.
evidence: This is based on comparative cell biology across prokaryotes.

claim: Eukaryotic traits are better understood as being selected for to service an endosymbiont and less so as means of acquiring one.
source: Reflecting on eukaryotic traits and their cell biological connection to mitochondrial origin lets us conclude they are better understood as being selected for to service an endosymbiont and less so as means of acquiring one.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on synthesis of evidence.

claim: Phylogeny guided models should connect interpretations to a physiological and cell biological rationale.
source: Phylogeny guided models should connect interpretations to a physiological and cell biological rationale, while facing the challenge of resolving the fluid nature of the pangenomes of both host and endosymbiont genome throughout eukaryogenesis – we need to talk to phylogenetic trees, not only about them.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation for the field.

claim: Physiology, geochemistry, phylogenetics, and culturing and imaging all point to a syntrophic origin of eukaryotes involving two prokaryotic partners.
source: Physiology (Imachi et al., 2020; Martin and Müller, 1998; Moreira, 1998; Spang et al., 2019), geochemistry (Mills et al., 2022), phylogenetics (Wu et al., 2022), and culturing and imaging (Imachi et al., 2020) all point to a syntrophic origin of eukaryotes involving two prokaryotic partners.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple lines of evidence with citations.

claim: The data suggests that first steps towards endosymbiosis in eukaryogenesis were of prokaryotic nature.
source: The data suggests that first steps towards endosymbiosis in eukaryogenesis were of prokaryotic nature, that eukaryogenesis likely only solidified upon endosymbiosis, and that hence the definition of FECA should include an endosymbiont.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on synthesis of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Eukaryogenesis likely only solidified upon endosymbiosis.
source: The data suggests that first steps towards endosymbiosis in eukaryogenesis were of prokaryotic nature, that eukaryogenesis likely only solidified upon endosymbiosis, and that hence the definition of FECA should include an endosymbiont.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on synthesis of multiple lines of evidence.
